h1: Arizona HOA Selective Enforcement Challenge Letter Generator
metaTitle: Arizona HOA Selective Enforcement Demand Letter
metaDescription: Generate an Arizona HOA selective enforcement challenge demand letter. Cite A.R.S. § 33-1803, halt unfair fines, and protect your homeowner rights today.
deadline: 21 calendar days to send a written response to a violation notice by certified mail; the HOA then has 10 business days to respond (A.R.S. § 33-1803(C)-(D))
penalty: Fines may be challenged through an ADRE petition (civil penalties and compliance orders) or in court; costs and attorney fees to the prevailing party in a lien action under A.R.S. § 33-1807(I)
introParagraph: If your Arizona HOA is fining you for something your neighbors do openly without consequence, you may have a valid selective enforcement claim. Arizona's Planned Communities Act gives homeowners specific protections against arbitrary, inconsistent, or discriminatory rule enforcement. Boards cannot pick and choose which residents to penalize while ignoring identical conduct elsewhere in the community. A well-crafted demand letter that cites Arizona Revised Statutes and documents the disparate treatment often resolves the dispute before it escalates to the Arizona Department of Real Estate (ADRE) or Superior Court. This page explains how Arizona law treats selective enforcement, the deadlines that apply, and how a properly drafted letter can stop the fines, reverse the violation, and force your board to enforce its rules uniformly going forward.
lawExplanation:
Arizona regulates homeowner associations through the Planned Communities Act (A.R.S. Title 33, Chapter 16) and the Condominium Act (Title 33, Chapter 9). Under A.R.S. § 33-1803(B), after notice and an opportunity to be heard, the board of directors may impose reasonable monetary penalties on members for violations of the declaration, bylaws and rules of the association. A member who receives a written notice that the condition of the member's property violates the community documents may send a written response by certified mail within twenty-one calendar days after the date of the notice (§ 33-1803(C)), and the association must respond in writing within ten business days with the provision allegedly violated, the date of the violation, who observed it, and the process for contesting the notice (§ 33-1803(D)).

Selective enforcement is a defense based on the equitable doctrine that a board may not enforce a covenant against one owner while knowingly tolerating identical violations by others; whether a court will treat a covenant as waived or unenforceable depends on the facts and on the governing documents, so documenting how others were treated differently is essential. Homeowners also have the right under A.R.S. § 33-1804 to attend open meetings of the association and board, and under A.R.S. § 33-1805 to examine the association's financial and other records, which can help prove disparate treatment.

If informal resolution fails, A.R.S. § 32-2199.01 lets an owner petition the Arizona Department of Real Estate for a hearing on violations of the planned community statutes or documents, or you may pursue claims in Justice Court or Superior Court. An administrative law judge may order a party to abide by the statute or documents and may levy a civil penalty (A.R.S. § 32-2199.02).
letterStrategy: An effective Arizona selective enforcement demand letter does three things: it documents the disparate treatment, cites the controlling statutes, and sets a firm deadline for corrective action. Start by identifying the specific covenant or rule the HOA claims you violated and quote it verbatim. Then list comparable violations elsewhere in the community—overgrown lawns, parked RVs, unapproved paint colors, holiday decorations left up too long—including addresses, photographs, and dates showing the board has taken no action. This evidence is the heart of your claim. Next, send your written response within the twenty-one calendar days allowed by A.R.S. § 33-1803(C), by certified mail to the address in the notice, and reference the open-meeting and records-examination rights under §§ 33-1804 and 33-1805 that you intend to exercise. Demand that the board (1) rescind the violation notice, (2) refund any fines paid, (3) remove the matter from your account, and (4) confirm in writing that the rule will be enforced uniformly going forward. Give the board 14 to 30 days to respond. Warn that continued enforcement may lead to an ADRE petition under A.R.S. § 32-2199.01 and a court action. Send the letter by certified mail, return receipt requested, and keep copies of every photograph and communication. Most Arizona boards back down once they see organized evidence and accurate statutory citations.
proceduralNotes: Arizona homeowners have several venues. The Arizona Department of Real Estate accepts HOA petitions for a filing fee set by the Department, with hearings before the Office of Administrative Hearings under A.R.S. § 32-2199.01. The small claims division of Justice Court handles claims up to $5,000 (A.R.S. § 22-503), and Justice Court has jurisdiction over civil actions up to $10,000 (A.R.S. § 22-201). Superior Court handles larger claims and injunctive relief. An action for debt founded on a written contract executed in Arizona must be brought within six years (A.R.S. § 12-548), but act quickly—evidence disappears. Send your response to the violation notice within the twenty-one-day window of A.R.S. § 33-1803(C) to preserve your position. In a lien action under A.R.S. § 33-1807, the judgment may include costs and reasonable attorney fees for the prevailing party.

faq.q: What counts as selective enforcement by an Arizona HOA?
faq.a: Selective enforcement occurs when your HOA penalizes you for conduct it knowingly ignores when other owners do the same thing. Examples include fining you for a parked truck while neighbors park identical trucks, citing your landscaping while overgrown yards on the same street go untouched, or enforcing paint-color rules only against certain homeowners. Whether inconsistent enforcement defeats a covenant as applied to you depends on the facts and the governing documents. Photographs, dates, addresses, and board meeting minutes are the strongest evidence to prove the pattern.

faq.q: How long do I have to respond to an Arizona HOA violation notice?
faq.a: Under A.R.S. § 33-1803(C), a member who receives a written notice that the condition of the member's property violates the community documents may respond by certified mail within twenty-one calendar days after the date of the notice. The association must then respond in writing within ten business days (§ 33-1803(D)). Send your response and demand letter by certified mail to create a paper trail. You may also petition for an administrative hearing with the Department of Real Estate under A.R.S. § 32-2199.01 at any time before or after that exchange of information, if the dispute is within its jurisdiction.

faq.q: Can I recover attorney's fees if I win?
faq.a: Possibly. In a lien action under A.R.S. § 33-1807, the judgment may include costs and reasonable attorney fees for the prevailing party, and a court may award reasonable attorney fees to the successful party in a contested action arising out of a contract (A.R.S. § 12-341.01). In an ADRE proceeding, the administrative law judge must order the respondent to pay the petitioner the filing fee if the petitioner prevails (A.R.S. § 32-2199.02). Keep records of your time and costs, and mention these provisions in your demand letter to put the board on notice that fee exposure runs both ways.

faq.q: Should I file with the ADRE or in court?
faq.a: It depends on the remedy you want. The Arizona Department of Real Estate hears petitions about violations of the planned community statutes or documents under A.R.S. § 32-2199.01, with a hearing before an administrative law judge; it is limited to those violations. Small claims (up to $5,000) is good for refunding paid fines. Superior Court is necessary for injunctive relief or larger damages. Many homeowners start with a demand letter, then file with ADRE if the board refuses to correct course.

faq.q: What evidence do I need to prove selective enforcement?
faq.a: Build a comparison file. Take dated, geotagged photographs of similar violations elsewhere in the community, noting addresses. Request the HOA's enforcement records and fining history under A.R.S. § 33-1805—the association has ten business days to fulfill a request to examine or to provide copies. Save board meeting minutes, neighbor statements, and prior correspondence. The goal is showing a pattern: identical conduct, no enforcement action, while you alone are fined. The more comparators you document, the stronger your waiver and selective enforcement defense becomes under Arizona law.
